pages.title: Languages of Odisha
pages.lead: Begin with a language you know, or one you want to understand. Follow its writing, books and speakers—and notice where a familiar name can mean something different.

paragraphs.text: Kui and Kuvi have separate entries in SCSTRTI’s catalogue of trilingual learning booklets. The same catalogue offers resources labelled Santali, Saora, Ho, Juang and Koya. These publications give you something specific to begin with: a named learning resource, rather than a general description of a community.

Follow each title into its own introduction. A similar spelling is a reason to look more closely, not to merge two names. A teaching booklet is also only one view of a language; it cannot stand for every speaker, locality or kind of writing.

Santali and Ol Chiki show why the distinction matters. The President’s Secretariat’s account of the 2026 Ol Chiki celebration credits Raghunath Murmu with creating the script in 1925. It also describes earlier use of Roman, Devanagari, Odia and Bengali scripts for Santali.

A date in the history of a script is not a birth date for the language. Nor does a script name tell you everything about the literature written in it. The Santali introduction follows the writing into named books and literary gatherings; the small specimen in this directory spells “Ol Chiki”, the script’s name.

When someone shares a word or expression, ask what they call their language, where they use it and who taught it to them. Keep that context with the example. A family’s name for its speech, a publication’s title and an administrative label may answer different questions.

Odia is the starting point for this collection, with other languages receiving their own introductions. The Sambalpuri page considers the names Sambalpuri and Kosali without treating their preferred use as settled for every speaker. The Desia page follows learning and theatre projects. These are paths to explore, not a complete inventory of Odisha’s languages.

sections.title: A page that asks you to look closer

paragraphs.text: The photograph shows an Odia palm-leaf manuscript and a lekhani, or writing stylus, at Gyana Mandira library in Koraput. It is one surviving object to look at closely, not a date for the birth of the language.

The government’s literary overview places Sarala Das’s Mahabharata in the fifteenth century and describes later traditions of narrative and devotional verse. Its modern survey includes Radhanath Ray, Gangadhar Meher and Fakir Mohan Senapati, followed by further poetic movements and voices.
Follow a writer into a work, then return to the language with something new to listen for. Our literature collection begins that journey.

CIIL lists a 2019 introduction to Odia language, literature and culture, edited by Sanjaya Kumar Bag, intended for non-native learners. It is a useful bibliographic starting point; we have inspected its catalogue record, not the full book.
The next layer will add reviewed pronunciation, phrases and recordings by speakers. This first page makes no claim to be a complete history or a language course.

sections.title: Ol Chiki: a script with a story

paragraphs.text: The President’s Secretariat’s account of the 2026 centenary celebration credits Pandit Raghunath Murmu with creating Ol Chiki in 1925. It describes earlier use of Roman, Devanagari, Odia and Bengali scripts for Santali.
The age of a script is not the age of the language. Nor does one script represent every speaker’s writing practice.

Sahitya Akademi’s Santali award register lists Nalha, a poetry collection by Gobinda Chandra Majhi, as its 2016 winner. It gives a reader a particular author and work to seek out, beyond a general introduction to the script.
Start with an edition a fluent reader recommends. Ask what its title means in context, who is speaking in a poem, and what a translation carries—or leaves behind.

On 21 May 2022, Sahitya Akademi held a symposium in Baripada with the Santali department of MSCBD University. Its annual report names Damayanti Beshra among the scholars discussing Santali language, script and literature.
Read about Mayurbhanj with a literary question in mind: which writers are people reading now? The recorded symposium is part of the city’s cultural history, not an event available to book.
1925 · The President’s Secretariat credits Raghunath Murmu with inventing Ol Chiki in this year.
16 February 2026 · A centenary celebration in New Delhi recognised the script and contemporary Santali literary work. The event date and the 1925 origin date are separate milestones.

pages.title: Fakir Mohan Senapati
pages.kicker: Literary lives · Odia language and Odisha
pages.lead: Writer, teacher, printer and defender of Odia. Follow Fakir Mohan Senapati from the classroom and the press to the everyday lives that fill his fiction.

paragraphs.text: Fakir Mohan Senapati (1843–1918) belonged to a world of classrooms, presses, princely-state offices and village society. Born on 13 January 1843 at Malikashapur near Balasore, he lost his parents young and grew up under his grandmother’s care. His limited formal schooling did not end his education: teaching, reading and work became routes into a wider intellectual life. He later served as a dewan in several Odisha princely states. These roles matter because his fiction repeatedly enters the practical world of property, accounts, status and dependence.

sections.title: Defending Odia in the classroom and the press

paragraphs.text: Odia’s place in education was being challenged during Senapati’s lifetime. Proposals to displace it in schooling made textbooks and public argument matters of collective identity. His response included writing Odia textbooks: children needed books through which their own language could remain a medium of learning.

He brought a printing press to Balasore in 1868 and published Sambada Bahika and Bodhadayini. His public-language work also included organising meetings and contributing articles to Utkal Dipika against the proposed removal of Odia. Classrooms, the press and public discussion were connected parts of his work.

sections.title: Language and the making of Odisha

paragraphs.text: Odia-speaking regions were administered across Bengal, the Central Provinces and Madras. The movement known as Desha Mishran Andolan sought to bring these regions under one political administration. The struggle over language and the movement for territorial unification therefore belonged to the same historical setting, even though local disputes had different causes.

Senapati died in 1918. Odisha became a separate province on 1 April 1936, bringing together portions of the then Bihar and Odisha Province, Madras Presidency and the Central Provinces. His language work belongs to the movement’s earlier cultural and educational foundations; the province’s creation was a later collective achievement.

Read the public work alongside the fiction. Making Odia available in a classroom and giving its everyday speakers a place in literature help us understand the breadth of his contribution. His legacy asks a continuing question: where do we make room for our language to be learned, read and used?

sections.title: Rebati: a child’s wish to learn

paragraphs.text: Rebati begins with a household, its small income, cows, garden and evening devotional reading. The girl is already a listener and singer before she becomes a pupil. Her father and the young teacher Basudev support her learning; her grandmother expects domestic skills instead. A pictured primer delights her. After epidemic deaths, the household also loses cattle and cultivation rights. The grandmother blames the girl’s education for the family’s calamities. This is a character’s explanation, not the story’s demonstrated cause. The narrative makes the wish to learn inseparable from affection, vulnerability and material loss.

sections.title: Chha Mana Atha Guntha: reputation and power

paragraphs.text: The novel introduces Ramachandra Mangaraj as both landlord and moneylender, wrapped in a reputation for religious observance. The narrator appears to defend him, then supplies details that make the defence increasingly doubtful. This is how the satire works: readers must hear the gap between a respectable description and what the scene reveals. In the opening of the Bhagia-and-Saria chapter, the narrator mocks educated men who know foreign genealogies but neglect their own neighbours and institutions. Local knowledge becomes a challenge to fashionable claims of learning. These readings come from particular passages, not a completed reading of the entire novel.

sections.title: Patent Medicine: the household behind the joke

paragraphs.text: Chandramani’s attempts to evade his wife Sulochana’s restrictions lead to a confrontation over his intoxication and conduct. The broom beating that gives the title its joke is followed by injury, her remorse and care, and a quieter household in which the couple read together. The story can be read for the tension between a wife’s authority, the expectation of wifely devotion and a husband’s irresponsibility. That reading keeps the discomfort alongside the comedy. It does not turn the fictional beating into a remedy or flatten Sulochana into a simple emblem of emancipation.

sections.title: Listen to how the story is told

paragraphs.text: Senapati’s prose invites the reader into a conversation. A narrator explains, defends, digresses, asks a question and sometimes exposes the weakness of his own apparent argument. In the inspected novel passages, humour depends on this movement between assertion and detail. Rebati offers a different register: household description and dialogue gradually give way to grief and isolation. Read these side by side. The range matters more than a general label such as “social realism”: how does a sentence invite laughter, sympathy or distrust?

His writing also includes the novels Mamu, Lachhama and Prayaschitta, poetry and an autobiography, Atma Jibana Charita. Mamu opens another route into bureaucratic and urban society; Lachhama takes a historical setting involving Maratha incursions; Prayaschitta examines expiation and social authority. The autobiography places his remembered life beside Odisha’s social world. These are orientation notes from the saved historical essay, not completed readings.

Begin with Rebati for the household and a child’s desire to learn. Follow with Patent Medicine for dialogue, comedy and unequal expectations within marriage. Then read the opening of Chha Mana Atha Guntha and its weaver-community passage: notice whom the narrator addresses and whose knowledge he challenges. Continue through the complete novel before treating these scenes as its whole argument. Read the autobiography alongside a chronology, allowing remembered experience and independently documented events to remain distinct.

sections.title: Balasore: a place behind the pages

paragraphs.text: Malikashapur near Balasore is the starting point of Senapati’s life; Balasore also belongs to the account of his printing work. These are documented connections to a real place. The villages and households of his fiction need their own reading, rather than an assumed match to a visitor’s map.
A book can begin a literary visit. Ask a local bookseller which edition or story readers return to. Memorial access, museum hours and a walking route still need current local verification.

The English edition Six Acres and a Third offers another way into Chha Mana Atha Guntha. Its translators are Rabi Shankar Mishra, Satya P. Mohanty, Jatindra K. Nayak and Paul St-Pierre. Translation and publication details help identify a copy; they are not the basis of the literary account above.

The original novel’s publication year is held open here: saved accounts give 1902 and 1905, and original serial and book imprints have not yet been inspected. The readings above use selected Odia passages, not a complete critical edition.

pages.lead: A small piece of land can reveal a very large world.

paragraphs.text: Fakir Mohan Senapati’s novel is set in Odisha in the 1830s. A changing landholding brings property, law and village society into view; the publisher introduces it as a humorous account of colonial rural life.

The UC Press paperback lists Rabi Shankar Mishra, Satya Mohanty, Jatindra N. Nayak and Paul St.-Pierre as translators. Its publication date is December 2005, with ISBN 9780520228832. This is the translation edition date, not the original novel’s first publication.

pages.title: Kui
pages.lead: A classroom, a short story, a language of home. Follow the words into everyday life.

sections.title: A language with its own place

paragraphs.text: CIIL classifies Kui as a South-Central Dravidian language spoken in Odisha and describes its relationship to Kuvi. This collection treats the two as separate languages.
A language name cannot tell you everything about a speaker. We will record locality and self-identification alongside each future contribution.
CIIL’s overview connects Kui with Kandhamal. The CIIL–NCERT primer credits teachers and contributors from places including Daringbadi, Balliguda and Tikabali.

Those credits make language work visible: people teach, review and prepare material for others to use. They are a useful starting point for learning, not a list of people offering visitor appointments.
ATLC’s catalogue lists Tahii, a Kui short-story collection by Anuj Mohan Pradhan, dated 2015. SCSTRTI also lists Kui supplementary readers and Pilanka Katha titles.
Begin with a title and ask a fluent reader how they would introduce it. The full stories, their settings and permissions still need review before we present excerpts.

The CIIL–NCERT Kui Primer dates its first edition to 9 March 2024. It introduces letters and basic numerals for early learners and adult literacy. The development credits include teachers from Kandhamal and Kui author Srikant Mallick.
A familiar word on a page can be a beginning. Open the primer with someone who reads Kui, then let their explanation lead the lesson.

pages.lead: One voice can find more than one way onto a page. Follow the words into everyday life.

paragraphs.text: CIIL uses Sora and also records Saora and Savara. It places the language in the South Munda group of the Austroasiatic family. We use Saora / Sora here while leaving room for speakers’ preferred names.
The CIIL overview locates speakers mainly in Gajapati, Rayagada and Ganjam in Odisha. These are broad connections, not exclusive language boundaries or a map of every community.

sections.title: More than one way to write

paragraphs.text: CIIL describes writing in Latin, Odia and Telugu scripts as well as Sorang Sompeng. It dates the latter’s creation to 1936 and associates its development with Malia Gomango and Mangei Gomango.
Script history and individual practice deserve careful listening. A letter chart cannot stand in for someone’s voice, faith or knowledge.
SCSTRTI’s catalogue offers Saora supplementary readers and Pilanka Katha titles.

sections.title: Writing and a life in education

Sahitya Akademi’s author profile identifies Jajnaseni as Ray’s reconstruction of Draupadi’s life. Her own website provides an English excerpt under that title.
Try this reading question: whose choices move to the centre when a story is told through someone previously seen from the outside? The question is our invitation, not a quotation from the novel.

pages.title: Bhima Bhoi
pages.lead: A poem can begin as a prayer and grow into a question for the whole world: whose suffering do we notice?

paragraphs.text: Sahitya Akademi’s monograph by Sitakant Mahapatra reads Bhima Bhoi’s poetry through the Mahima faith and a powerful concern for human suffering. Compassion offers a starting point for approaching this nineteenth-century Odia poet.
Read slowly. Which lines address the divine, and which turn our attention back towards another person? This is an invitation to read, not a quotation from the poet.

Sambalpur district’s literary account lists Stuti Chintamani, Sruti Nisedha Gita, Ashtaka Bihari Gita and Bhajanamal among his works. The Akademi monograph offers a guided route into the writing and its interpretation.
Use a named edition and keep the translator’s credit beside any translation. Recordings and accurately checked Odia excerpts can deepen this page in a later editorial pass.

Mahapatra’s account connects Khaliapali with Bhima Bhoi’s later religious and literary activity. The photograph here shows a memorial setting, not the poet himself or a reconstruction of his lifetime.
Treat a future visit as a visit to a living place of devotion. Ask locally about access, observances and photography before going; we have not inspected visitor arrangements.

The monograph opens by noting uncertainty about his exact birth date, birthplace and the history of his blindness. This introduction leaves those questions open instead of selecting one account as certain.

pages.title: Gopinath Mohanty
pages.lead: A landscape holds more than a view. Follow a novelist into the lives, speech and unequal choices that give a place its human depth.

paragraphs.text: The author’s memorial website places his birth in Nagabali, Cuttack, in 1914. It describes an administrative career that began in 1938 and early work in Koraput, where he took an interest in local languages and lives.
Carry that connection as a reading question: how does someone’s work in a place shape what they notice—and what might their perspective leave out?

The memorial website describes Paraja through conflict between exploitation and those subjected to it, and credits Bikram Das with its English translation. Oxford University Press lists an English edition under Gopinath Mohanty’s name.
A novel is a crafted literary world. Read it alongside present-day voices from the communities concerned, rather than treating its characters as a guide to every person you meet.
The life sketch also names Amrutara Santana and Mati Matala among his major novels, and describes his interest in everyday speech, translation and language research.
Choose one work first. Note the edition and translator, then follow a recurring image, a conversation or a character’s decision through the book.
The memorial website includes interview and conversation links. They offer a listening route alongside the reading; the recordings remain with their hosts.

pages.title: Juang
pages.lead: A house of memory. A language of its own. Follow the words into everyday life.

paragraphs.text: CIIL identifies Juang as a Munda language within the Austroasiatic family, spoken in parts of Keonjhar, Angul and Dhenkanal. Juang is the language’s name; Munda describes a wider language group.
This is a starting point, not a complete map of speakers. Community identity, home language and the language someone uses at school or work need not be the same.
CIIL also describes Juang being written in the Odia script. A shared writing system is a bridge for readers; it does not make the languages identical.

SCSTRTI describes the majang, also called mandaghar, as a community institution with roles in gatherings, music and shared resources. Its account also records an origin belief connecting ancestors to Rusi Tangar near Gonasika. This is a reported tradition, not an archaeological finding.

Begin with a story its teller wants to share. Ask how place names are pronounced, who taught the story and whether it is appropriate to publish. A public retelling should keep the teller’s context, credit and choice of words.

pages.title: Gangadhar Meher
pages.lead: A loom makes a world from threads. A poem makes one from words. Meet a poet whose life invites you to think about both kinds of making.
pages.identity_note: An editorial reading panel, not a portrait or quotation.

paragraphs.text: Sambalpur district’s account places Gangadhar Meher’s birth in Barpali, now in Bargarh district, in a weaving family. It remembers him under the name Swabhaba Kabi.

Hold craft and poetry together as a reading question. How does attention—to a line, a pattern, a rhythm—change what we notice? This comparison is our invitation, not a statement attributed to the poet.

sections.title: An old story can become a new poem

paragraphs.text: The Odisha government’s literary overview connects Meher’s themes to the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and other classical sources. His work offers a route into the continuing conversation between Odia poetry and epic narrative.

Sambalpur district lists Pranaya Ballari, Kichaka Badha and Indumati among his works. Ask a library or bookseller for a reliable edition of one title, with an introduction that explains its literary setting.

Choose a reliable edition with a named editor or translator. Follow one scene and ask what its sound, images and point of view make you feel. Keep a translation’s interpretation distinct from the original words.

sections.title: Follow the name back to a place

paragraphs.text: Barpali is a useful beginning for researching his life. A birthplace connection is not a promise that a house, memorial or library is currently open to visitors. Check arrangements locally before making a special trip.
If you know a local reading group, an accessible edition or an accurately credited recording, help us add that next layer. We have not yet selected an excerpt or recording for reproduction.

Try another Odia writer alongside Meher. What changes when a work addresses everyday lives, devotion or a familiar epic? Our profiles are starting points; the pleasure lies in returning to the writing itself.

pages.title: Sambalpuri
pages.kicker: Western Odisha · song · a language of belonging
pages.lead: A song can reach you before a map does. Begin with its makers, then listen for the world around it.
identity_panel: A song. A voice. A place.

paragraphs.text: Sambalpur district’s cultural account describes Sambalpuri as spoken in western Odisha and distinguishes it from speech in coastal districts. Its account places language beside music, dance and festivals.
Sambalpuri and Kosali are names readers may encounter. We preserve the wording of each source rather than treating the names, their extent or their preferred use as settled for every speaker.

A January 2022 Odisha Review interview with lyricist Mitrabhanu Gountia connects “Rangabati” with composer Prabhudatta Pradhan and singers Jitendriya Haripal and Krishna Patel. The account traces the song through All India Radio, Sambalpur, and a later commercial recording.

Gountia recalls turning towards writing in his mother tongue and describes a wider literary life of lyrics, plays and prose. Read this as a writer’s account of his practice and aspirations, not a complete history of the language.
When you find an authorised recording, keep the lyricist, composer, singers and version together. A familiar refrain becomes richer when its makers remain visible.

The district account connects Nuakhai with new rice, family gatherings and greetings, and describes Dalkhai through song and dance. These are cultural connections to explore with local context, not a programme of performances available on demand.
Ask a willing reader for a poem they return to, or a host about a greeting used in their own family. Leave space for an answer that differs from the printed description.

reading_notes.heading: Follow the makers
reading_notes.text: The 2022 interview names Mitrabhanu Gountia, Prabhudatta Pradhan, Jitendriya Haripal and Krishna Patel. Keep creator and recording-version credits together.

reading_notes.heading: A label is a starting point
reading_notes.text: Ask which name and local variety a speaker uses. Census 2011 lists Sambalpuri within the ODIA group; this does not settle community identity.

pages.review: Source-linked English introduction. Community-preferred naming, fluent-speaker review and a fuller literary history remain open. No original-language phrases, translated lyrics or recordings are reproduced.
pages.identity_note: A reading doorway; a Census label is not the last word on identity.
pages.title: Desia
pages.lead: A language belongs on a stage and in a child’s first book. Follow two documented moments in Desia’s continuing story.
identity_panel: Listen to the people behind the name

paragraphs.text: The Census entry Desia gives this introduction a statistical starting point. It does not make every related name interchangeable. SCSTRTI’s learning catalogue also uses Bhatri-Desia; the relationship between these labels needs speaker and specialist context.
Our population panel uses only the entry explicitly labelled Desia. It does not absorb Bhatri, infer ancestry or draw a boundary around every person who uses Desia.

On 2 June 2023, the Ministry of Education reported a workshop involving NCERT’s Regional Institute of Education, Bhubaneswar, and the Central University of Odisha. Participants prepared learning materials in Kui and Desia, with listening, speaking, reading and writing in view. The release described testing and revision still to come.

The moment matters: a language familiar at home was being considered for the first steps of classroom learning. The report is evidence of that work in 2023, not a guarantee that a particular book is available today.

SCSTRTI’s January–June 2024 newsletter reports multilingual dramas in Santali, Mundari, Desia and Ho at Adivasi Mela 2024 in Bhubaneswar. The same newsletter lists school learning publications spanning Desia, Koya, Sadri and Ho.

A classroom and a stage offer two doors into this story. With a willing teacher, reader or performer, ask what they read, how they name their language and which stories they want to carry forward. A fuller history of Desia literature and oral traditions needs named works, tellers and versions.

reading_notes.heading: Keep publication stages clear
reading_notes.text: The June 2023 workshop report described preparation and future testing. Confirm a book’s edition and availability before planning to use it.

reading_notes.heading: Ask for a story and its context
reading_notes.text: Keep the teller, locality, date, language name, version and permission alongside any shared account. The 2024 drama report is historical, not a current performance listing.
